chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Rasool-Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Aal) said: There is no prohibition (hurma) for the women of the Ahl al-Zimma that one should not look at their hair and their hands.

key_terms.أَهْلِ الذِّمَّةِ: Ahl al-Zimma; people under covenant/protection, typically non-Muslims living in an Islamic state
key_terms.حُرْمَة: Hurma; sanctity, prohibition, or right of concealment (awrah)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on looking at the hair and hands of Ahl al-Zimma women in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the fiqh of 'hurma' (sanctity of concealment) regarding the women of the Ahl al-Zimma, establishing that their hair and hands are not considered awrah in the same strict sense as for Muslim women. Historically, this ruling facilitated social and economic interactions in early Islamic societies by defining the boundaries of modesty for non-Muslim residents under Islamic protection. It reflects the Shia scholarly view that legal obligations of hijab are tied to religious identity, distinguishing between the general public gaze and the specific requirements of prayer or marriage.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Al Nowfaly, from Al Sakuny, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘Rasool-Allahsaww said: ‘There is no Prohibition to look at the women of the Ahl Al-Zimma if one looks at their hair and their hands’.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from af-Nawfafiy from af-Sakuniy who has said the following: “

The Messenger of Allah, O Allah, grant compensation to Muhammad and his family worthy of their services to Your cause, has said, ‘It is not unlawful for one to look at the hairs and hands of the taxpayer women.’”
